identity.name: Cis-Sutlej states
native_names: ਸਤਲੁਜ ਦੇ ਇਸ ਪਾਰ ਦੀਆਂ ਰਿਆਸਤਾਂ (Satluj de is pār dīāṁ riāsatāṁ)

land.text: Sirhind and the country between the Sutlej and the Yamuna, handed to Ala Singh of Patiala and the other chiefs after 1764 (the sikh-confederacy 1764 keyframe), up to the confederacy's end in 1799

predecessors.note: The Cis-Sutlej page: Ala Singh of Patiala 'had been conquering territory from circa 1730 onwards'; the Maratha-Sikh treaty of 10 May 1785 made the small Cis-Sutlej states an autonomous protectorate of Scindia, which 'broke down'. The dossier starts in 1800, the year after the sikh-confederacy dossier ends, so that the land is not nobody's.

land.text: the land 'between the Sutlej River on the north, the Himalayas on the east' and 'the Yamuna River and Delhi District on the south', Sirsa District on the west: Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Kalsia, Ladwa, Faridkot, Malerkotla and the rest, as Cliopatria's British Empire 1811 step draws the Cis-Sutlej states (India part)

successors.note: 1849: the Punjab 'was annexed to British India, and the Cis-Sutlej commissionership was incorporated with the new Punjab Province' (Ambala, Ferozepore, Ludhiana, Thanesar, Simla). The chiefs' states stayed as princely states under British paramountcy: Patiala, Jind, Nabha and the rest, except Kaithal, 'would join PEPSU' after Indian independence (no date on the page). No dossier holds them after 1849.

capitals.name: Patiala (leading chief's seat)
capitals.note: The page gives no capital for the group. Patiala is the founder-state (Ala Singh) and the largest of the Phulkian states, used as a marker only; each chief had his own seat (Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Ladwa, Faridkot).

correction.text: the land 'between the Sutlej River on the north, the Himalayas on the east' and 'the Yamuna River and Delhi District on the south', Sirsa District on the west: Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Kalsia, Ladwa, Faridkot, Malerkotla and the rest, as Cliopatria's British Empire 1811 step draws the Cis-Sutlej states (India part)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (no Cliopatria shape; Cliopatria's Sikh Confederacy shapes of 1800-1806 are the Amritsar remnant, and the land is nobody's until its British Empire shape of 1811). The page names the bounds (the Sutlej north, the Himalayas east, the Yamuna and Delhi District south, Sirsa district west) and the states 'among others': Kalsia, Kaithal, Patiala, Nabha, Jind, Thanesar, Malerkotla, Ludhiana, Kapurthala, Ladwa, Ambala, Ferozepur and Faridkot; no area is given. The 197-cell (about 49,800 km2) region is the Indian part of the British Empire 1811 step less its 1809 shape; Hisar, Panipat and Rohtak (Delhi District) went to the British in 1803 and are outside. Kapurthala sits in the Trans-Sutlej group on the same page and is not separated.

minus.text: Ambala and Faridkot, taken by Ranjit Singh's third expedition

correction.text: the Cis-Sutlej lands of 1800-1807 less Ambala and Faridkot, 'took-control of' by Ranjit Singh in 1808

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for the one year of Sikh Empire control (the page: Ranjit Singh's third expedition took Ambala and Faridkot). Faridkot is a coordinate disc (not in the gazetteer).

minus.text: the Cis-Sutlej lands under British protection
the 'large territory along river Sutlej from Chamkaur to Harikepatan' that Ochterlony recognised as Ranjit Singh's

correction.text: the Cis-Sutlej lands from 1809 under British protection, less the strip on the Sutlej that Ranjit Singh kept (29 July 1809)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1809-1849. The Treaty of Amritsar (25 April 1809) 'pushed the boundary of British India from the Yamuna to the Sutlej' and Ranjit Singh vacated Faridkot and Ambala. The British Empire dossier's own ledger dates the protectorate 1815, the page 1809; the Sikh Empire kept the Sutlej strip until 1846, which the page does not date. The Cis-Sutlej commissionership (Ambala, Ferozepore, Ludhiana, Thanesar, Simla) ran to 1849.

region.text: the land 'between the Sutlej River on the north, the Himalayas on the east' and 'the Yamuna River and Delhi District on the south', Sirsa District on the west: Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Kalsia, Ladwa, Faridkot, Malerkotla and the rest, as Cliopatria's British Empire 1811 step draws the Cis-Sutlej states (India part)

ledger.note: 1800: the Phulkian and other Sikh chiefs between the Sutlej and the Yamuna stand on their own after the Sikh Confederacy ends. The page is silent on 1800: it gives Ala Singh's conquests 'from circa 1730 onwards', the 1785 Maratha-Sikh protectorate (10 May 1785) that broke down, the British-Scindia settlement of 20 December 1803 and 27 February 1804, and '1 January 1806: The Treaty of Lahore kept the Marathas out of the Punjab'. The start is the year after sikh-confederacy ends (1799), a bridging judgment.

region.text: Ludhiana, 'captured' by Ranjit Singh on 26 July 1806 and handed to Raja Bhag Singh of Jind

ledger.note: 26 July 1806: Ranjit Singh crosses the Sutlej and takes Ludhiana. 'Ranjit Singh's forces crossed the Sutlej and captured Ludhiana'; 'control over the captured Ludhiana being given-over to Raja Bhag Singh of Jind State'. The first of 'three expeditions into Cis-Sutlej states in 1806, 1807 and 1808'; in 1807 'local chiefs of the Sirhind region asked the British for protection'. The sikh-empire ledger has no matching contest.

region.text: Ambala and Faridkot, taken by Ranjit Singh's third expedition

ledger.note: 1808: Ranjit Singh's third expedition takes Ambala and Faridkot. The page puts it in September 1808, when 'fearing a French invasion, the British sent Charles Metcalfe to Lahore' and the expedition 'took Ambala and Faridkot in the same period'; the month of the capture is not given.

region.text: Ambala and Faridkot, vacated by Ranjit Singh under the Treaty of Amritsar

ledger.note: 25 April 1809: Ranjit Singh gives Ambala and Faridkot back. 'Ranjit Singh had vacated his control over Faridkot and Ambala'; the treaty fixes the Sutlej as the border ('permitted him complete freedom of action to the north of it'); the article gives 26 April for the treaty text and a proclamation of 3 May 1809; Ochterlony's announcement that the Cis-Sutlej chiefs 'were now under British protection' is dated 12 June 1809. The British Empire ledger books the same gain.

region.text: Ludhiana and the Sirhind lands, after the Treaty of Amritsar

ledger.note: 25 April 1809: the Treaty of Amritsar ends the Sikh Empire's push south of the Sutlej and puts the Cis-Sutlej chiefs under British protection (the page's infobox dates the British protectorate to 1809; the proclamation was 3 May 1809, Ochterlony's announcement 12 June 1809). The protectorate tint belongs in the British Empire / East India Company ledger as a vassal_start for this slug (see notes).

region.text: 'large territory along river Sutlej from Chamkaur to Harikepatan' recognised as Ranjit Singh's

ledger.note: 29 July 1809: Ochterlony recognises Ranjit Singh's hold on the south bank of the Sutlej from Chamkaur to Harike Patan, 'and other chiefs received villages as rewards'. The page does not date Ranjit Singh's acquisition of the strip, which he 'kept' from before the third expedition (1806-1808); the date here is the recognition.

region.text: the land 'between the Sutlej River on the north, the Himalayas on the east' and 'the Yamuna River and Delhi District on the south', Sirsa District on the west: Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Kalsia, Ladwa, Faridkot, Malerkotla and the rest, as Cliopatria's British Empire 1811 step draws the Cis-Sutlej states (India part)

ledger.note: 1849: the Cis-Sutlej commissionership joins the new Punjab Province. 'In 1849, the Punjab was annexed to British India, and the Cis-Sutlej commissionership was incorporated with the new Punjab Province'; the name Cis-Sutlej was used for the division until 1862. The British Empire dossier dates the annexation of the Punjab 2 April 1849. The princely states of Patiala, Jind and Nabha stayed as states under the Crown until after 1947.

wars.name: Ranjit Singh's expeditions into the Cis-Sutlej states (1806, 1807, 1808)
wars.outcome: Ranjit Singh took Ludhiana (26 July 1806, handed to Jind), then Ambala and Faridkot (1808); the chiefs called in the British, and the Treaty of Amritsar (25 April 1809) fixed the Sutlej as the frontier, Ranjit Singh vacated Ambala and Faridkot and kept the Sutlej strip (29 July 1809).
wars.note: Cis-Sutlej page: 'led three expeditions into Cis-Sutlej states in 1806, 1807 and 1808'; 'In 1807 ... local chiefs of the Sirhind region asked the British for protection.' The 9 February 1809 warning of Ochterlony ended further incursions. The 1807 gains are not named on the page.

certainty.note: The page names bounds and states but no lines: the Sutlej and the Yamuna are the only fixed edges; the inner boundaries between chiefs are not given and the region is drawn from Cliopatria's British Empire step.

Sharp only along the Sutlej, fixed by the Treaty of Amritsar (25 April 1809) and the 1809 recognition of Ranjit Singh's strip; the Yamuna and Delhi District edge and the lines between the Phulkian chiefs and the British districts remain approximate.

sources.title: Cis-Sutlej states
sources.note: Bounds and the list of states, the 1785 Maratha-Sikh protectorate, the 1803-1806 British and Maratha treaties, Ranjit Singh's expeditions of 1806-1808, the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar, the 29 July 1809 recognition, 1849 incorporation, PEPSU. No area, no capital, no founding date of the states.

sources.title: Treaty of Amritsar (1809)
sources.note: 25 April 1809 (26 April in the treaty text), the Sutlej as frontier, 3 May 1809 proclamation, 12 June 1809 announcement of British protection to the Cis-Sutlej chiefs, Faridkot and Ambala vacated. Does not name Patiala, Jind, Nabha or Kaithal.

notes: Requested by the p1800-p1809 window (about 130 cells of Indian Punjab and Haryana nobody's: the sikh-confederacy dossier ends 1799 and the Sikh Empire holds only the north). Range and region: the dossier starts in 1800, the year after the sikh-confederacy dossier ends, and draws the Cis-Sutlej lands as the Indian part of Cliopatria's British Empire 1811 step less its 1809 shape (197 cells, about 49,800 km2); the page names the bounds and some of the states but no area, no capital and no founding date. Each state (Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Kalsia, Ladwa, Faridkot, Malerkotla, Thanesar, Ludhiana) is only a name here: a state-by-state split would need pages on each. Protectorate: the pages put the British protection at 1809 (infobox; 3 May proclamation; Ochterlony's announcement of 12 June 1809), but the british-empire ledger books a vassal_start for 'Cis-Sutlej states' in 1815 and the east-india-company ledger one for 'Cis-Sutlej Hill States' in 1815: both should read cis-sutlej-states with the 1809 date (tint, rule 4); a vassal event cannot be in this dossier because the counterpart of a vassal event is the vassal and it belongs to the suzerain's ledger. The sikh-empire ledger has no loss/contest for the 1806-1809 expeditions and the Sutlej strip; the british-empire dossier lists Cliopatria's 1811 step as a 1815 vassal tint. Kapurthala: the page lists it among the Cis-Sutlej states but the Bist Doab (Kapurthala) is Trans-Sutlej (merged into a Trans-Sutlej state in 1846): not separated. 1846 (Treaty of Lahore) 'annexed the Jalandhar Doab' to the British and the Sikh Empire's Cis-Sutlej strip; no page opened dates the strip's passage, so it stays in the Sikh Empire's ledger. Princely states after 1849 (Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Malerkotla, Kalsia, Faridkot; PEPSU 1948-56) have no dossier. Gazetteer names needed: Faridkot, Jind, Kaithal, Nabha, Malerkotla, Kalsia, Ladwa, Thanesar, Sirhind (place or region). Wikidata id not known.
